paras: The threatened lynching of Willis Martin occurred in October 1903 at DeKalb, Mississippi, when a crowd of masked men gathered at night to seize Martin, a Black prisoner held in the town jail after a cutting fight. The crowd dispersed on learning that Sheriff Hull had placed special deputies around the jail, and the next day the sheriff moved Martin to the jail at Macon. The episode is known from a single Kemper Herald item reprinted in the Macon Beacon.

According to the Kemper Herald, Ben Martin and his son Willis, both described as "colored," had repeatedly left down the bars in the fence on Hute Shumate's place, about eleven miles northwest of DeKalb, and Shumate had objected several times. On a Friday evening, probably 23 October, Shumate and his son Eli found the fence down again and spoke to the Martins in a nearby field. The paper said the Martins were "impudent" and that a fight followed, without saying who struck first.
Hute Shumate and Ben Martin were so badly cut that they were not expected to recover, Eli Shumate was "dangerously if not fatally cut," and Willis Martin received slight cuts.

Willis Martin was placed in the jail at DeKalb on Saturday, and that night "a crowd of masked men" gathered in the town "with the evident intention of lynching the prisoner." Sheriff Hull had been warned in time and had a large force of special deputies guarding the jail; on learning this, the crowd dispersed. "To prevent further trouble," the sheriff and A. A. Overstreet took Martin to Macon on Sunday and lodged him in jail there "for safe keeping."
No arrests of the masked men are reported, and the coverage does not show whether Martin was tried or whether the wounded men died.

The story appeared as a local item headed "Serious Cutting Affray" in the Kemper Herald and was reprinted, with credit, in the Macon Beacon of 31 October 1903. The item placed the cause of the fight on the Martins' "impudent" reply and opened by forecasting "the death of three men" and "the hanging of the fourth," treating a legal execution of Willis Martin as a likely outcome. It called the masked men "the mob" and reported the sheriff's guard and the transfer to Macon without editorial comment.
No wire report or Black-press coverage of the episode was found beyond the Macon Beacon reprint.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Willis Martin
bases: A crowd of masked men gathered at DeKalb 'with the evident intention of lynching' Willis Martin, a jailed Black prisoner, and dispersed when they learned the jail was guarded (A2); a threatened lynching.

The only report is one Kemper Herald item, known through its reprint in the Macon Beacon (A2); the item linked to the event in the Kemper Herald is an advertisement (A1), and no other paper was found.

accounts.label: Kemper Herald (local weekly), reprinted by the Macon Beacon
accounts.gist: After the Martins left down fence bars on Shumate's place and were 'impudent' when spoken to, a cutting fight left three men badly hurt; masked men gathered to lynch Willis Martin at the DeKalb jail but dispersed when they found it guarded, and the sheriff moved him to Macon.

framing.detail: Headed 'Serious Cutting Affray', the item put the fight down to the Martins being 'impudent' and anticipated 'the hanging of the fourth', while describing the masked crowd as 'the mob' and noting the sheriff's guard and transfer without further comment.

record_check.dossier: Willis Martin (son of Ben Martin); the record reverses the name.
lynching (threatened): a masked crowd gathered to lynch a jailed prisoner.
Held after a cutting fight with Hute and Eli Shumate in which three men were badly hurt; no formal charge named.
mob: 'a crowd of masked men', 'the mob'; no organized band named.
Not named in the text; the story came from the Kemper Herald, which is consistent with the record.
The linked Kemper Herald item is a patent-medicine advertisement (A1); the supporting text is the Macon Beacon's 1903-10-31 reprint of the Kemper Herald item (A2).

record_check.record: Masked men gathered ... sheriff moved the prisoner to Macon.
record_check.dossier: Supported, with the name corrected to Willis Martin and the sheriff named as Hull.

info: Fight on a Friday evening; Willis Martin jailed at DeKalb on Saturday and the masked crowd gathered that night; moved to Macon on Sunday. Counting back from the Kemper Herald's weekly issue (reprinted 31 Oct.), the days are about 23, 24 and 25 Oct. 1903.
Fight on Hute Shumate's place, about eleven miles northwest of DeKalb; crowd gathered in DeKalb, where Martin was jailed; prisoner moved to the jail at Macon.
Willis Martin, 'colored', son of Ben Martin; he had received 'some slight cuts' in the fight.

Held after a cutting fight in which Hute Shumate and Ben Martin were badly cut and Eli Shumate dangerously cut; the paper said the Martins had been 'impudent' when spoken to about fence bars left down. No formal charge is named.
'A crowd of masked men', called 'the mob'; no names and no race given.
0 by the mob; the paper said Ben Martin was not expected to recover from wounds in the fight.
The crowd dispersed and Martin was moved to Macon; no report of his trial or of the wounded men's fate was found.
